learningObjective: Use each training phase as an evidence gate, and return to the earliest failed assumption instead of tuning around an unverified pipeline.
mediumRationale: A compact Mermaid flowchart is the smallest medium that can show the recipe's ordered phases, the evidence required to advance, and the backward path when a gate fails. The task is procedural dependency rather than quantitative geometry, so labelled branches communicate the stop-and-repair discipline directly.

mediumComparison.mermaid: Selected: a top-to-bottom decision flow makes prerequisite gates and repair loops explicit while reusing the site's accessible, responsive process-diagram grammar.
mediumComparison.svg: Rejected: custom fixed geometry would duplicate Mermaid's existing flow and branch semantics without adding a quantitative shape or spatial relationship.
mediumComparison.semanticHtml: Rejected: a checklist or table can preserve order but cannot show that a failed gate routes backward and blocks all later tuning work as efficiently.
mediumComparison.interaction: Rejected: revealing stages or simulating choices would add controls and runtime behavior to a deterministic procedure whose complete logic fits in one compact flow.
mediumComparison.paperReuse: Rejected: the deck closely follows Karpathy's written recipe, but no source figure is necessary and permissive artwork-reuse rights were not established for the blog, course notes, or textbook. The diagram structure and wording are original.
mediumComparison.noVisual: Rejected: prose names six ordered steps, but readers can still treat them as an interchangeable checklist. A gate diagram exposes the central rule that later work is invalid until earlier evidence passes.

pages.insight: The preceding slide concludes the gradient-estimator section with control variates and provides no project-level training sequence.
The section divider announces Practical steps to a neural net project and establishes the exact local deck sequence reviewed for this article.
The notes slide collects preprocessing, initialization, numerical, and regularization cautions, but presents them as independent facts rather than advancement gates.
Data Inspection is explicitly first and asks the practitioner to inspect imbalance, bias, label noise, outliers, and the structure that should shape later architecture choices.

Setup training skeleton says to gain trust through explicit experiments, including correct initial loss, input-independent baselines, exact pre-model tensors, prediction dynamics, and overfitting a single batch before proceeding.
Sanity checks repeats the chance-loss and tiny-subset tests and uses training-versus-validation behavior to separate overfitting from insufficient capacity.
Finding the right model (a) says to minimize bias first with enough capacity to overfit, a simple known architecture, fixed seeds, and one change at a time.
Finding the right model (b) moves to variance reduction only after fitting, prioritizing more data, augmentation, pretraining, weight decay, early stopping, and related regularizers.
Squeeze juice out and debug places hyperparameter search and ensembling after the earlier phases and specifically argues for random rather than grid search.
The following slide starts Basic Probabilistic ML algorithms, confirming that the practical training recipe ends on page 63.

deckReview.notes: All 214 pages of the local deck were text-indexed for training recipe, practical steps, overfit, single or tiny batch, regularization, random search, grid search, sanity checks, and hyperparameters. The complete relevant section spans pages 56-63, so both boundary neighbors, pages 55 and 64, were inspected as well. Pages 58-63 closely parallel the article's inspect, verify, fit, regularize, tune, and squeeze order. No deck artwork, layout, examples, or wording is reused.

sources.title: A Recipe for Training Neural Networks
sources.usage: Used as the article's directly acknowledged practitioner source to verify the build-from-simple-to-complex process, explicit hypothesis checks, single-batch overfit gate, fit-before-regularize split, and late tuning stage.
sources.license: The author-hosted post is publicly readable, but no explicit permissive license for its prose or graphics was identified. No prose, artwork, layout, or examples are copied; the original diagram independently summarizes the procedure and links to the source.

sources.title: Deep Learning, Chapter 11: Practical Methodology
sources.usage: Used as an authoritative textbook source for the staged practical methodology of setting goals, establishing an end-to-end system, diagnosing bias and variance, and iterating under measured evidence.
sources.license: The online book is published by MIT Press and no permissive figure-reuse license was identified on the reviewed chapter. No text, figure, data, or chapter layout is reused.

sources.title: Random Search for Hyper-Parameter Optimization
sources.usage: Used as the primary research source for the article's late-stage recommendation that random search covers influential hyperparameters more efficiently than grid search under a fixed trial budget.
sources.license: JMLR papers are published under the journal's CC BY 4.0 license agreement. No paper figure, text, experiment, or layout is reused; the paper supports one terminal phase of the independently designed process diagram.

sourceReview.notes: The hardest mental model is that the phases are evidence-gated prerequisites rather than six independent optimization ideas. The original diagram therefore asks four pass/fail questions: whether data and baselines are trustworthy, whether a tiny batch can be memorized, whether the full training set can be fit, and whether validation behavior is acceptable after regularization. A no branch repairs the earliest failed assumption; random search and squeezing appear only after every gate passes. This is a procedural synthesis, not an empirical performance claim.

agentReview.summary: Read the complete article, text-indexed all 214 deck pages and inspected the entire practical-training section with both boundary neighbors, then checked the acknowledged practitioner recipe, an authoritative deep-learning textbook, and the primary random-search paper before selecting an original evidence-gate flowchart.

implementation.accessibility: The Mermaid diagram includes a concise accessible title and a full description of every phase, pass condition, and repair loop. Node text, gate shapes, labelled yes/no branches, line weight, and order carry the lesson without color. The established wide-diagram primitive preserves readable labels inside a keyboard-accessible horizontal scroller at 390 CSS pixels, while the direct caption states the full inference outside the scroller; shared Mermaid theme and print rules provide dark-mode contrast and remove the minimum width for a light printable layout.
